title: Grab 4 Socks: How Many Sets Have a Pair? | AMC 8-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: A drawer with 10 socks: 5 colors (red, blue, green, purple, orange), two of each, drawn as simple sock shapes. Line 1: a hand grabs 4 socks; two match and sparkle. Line 2: the 4 socks shuffle into a different grab with no match. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: Grab four socks from a drawer of five pairs. How often do you get a matching pair?
Counting the matches head-on gets messy. Counting the NON-matches is much easier.
Hello, I'm Vantee, and today we're sorting socks!

scenes.visual: Question text left; drawer of 10 socks right (5 colors × 2). Line 3: 4 socks lift out. Line 4: a matching pair glows. Line 5: chips 80, 125, 130, 140, 210.
lines: Here's the question.
A drawer has five pairs of socks, and each pair is a different color.
Zoe pulls out four socks.
How many sets of four socks contain at least one matching pair?
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: '10 socks: 5 colors × 2'; the two socks of one color look slightly different (stripe on one) to show they are different socks. Line 2: 'a SET: order doesn't matter'. Line 3: two example sets: 'one pair' and 'two pairs', both green ticks.
lines: So what do we know? Ten socks in all, two of each color. Each sock is its own sock.
A set of four is just which socks she holds. The order doesn't matter.
At least one pair means one matching pair, or even two pairs. Both count.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; drawer visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Right panel equation rows. Line 2: 'all sets − no-pair sets'. Line 3: '10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040'. Line 4: one set of 4 socks shown shuffling into a few orders; '4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 orders'. Line 5: '5040 ÷ 24 = 210'.
lines: Welcome back! Here's the strategy: count everything, then take away the sets with no pair.
All sets minus no-pair sets leaves the sets with a pair.
First, all sets. Pick socks one at a time: ten choices, then nine, then eight, then seven.
That's five thousand forty.
But each set got counted once for every order.
Four socks can line up in four times three times two times one, twenty-four orders.
So five thousand forty divided by twenty-four is two hundred ten sets in all.

scenes.visual: Line 1: no-pair set: 4 socks of 4 different colors. Line 2: 5 color dots, one left out at a time: '5 ways'. Line 3: each of the 4 chosen colors flips between its two socks: '2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16'. Line 4: '5 × 16 = 80'. Line 5: '210 − 80 = 130'. Line 6: answer badge '130' with chime at line end, choice C highlighted.
lines: Now the no-pair sets. No pair means four different colors.
Choose four of the five colors. That's the same as choosing the one color to leave out: five ways.
Each chosen color has two socks to pick from. Two times two times two times two is sixteen.
So there are five times sixteen, eighty sets with no pair.
Two hundred ten minus eighty is one hundred thirty.
One hundred thirty sets have a pair. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Two groups. Line 2: exactly one pair: pick pair color '5', two other colors from the remaining 4: list them '6 ways', a sock of each '2 × 2 = 4'; row '5 × 6 × 4 = 120'. Line 3: two pairs: the 10 color-pairs listed as small dot pairs; '10'. Line 4: '120 + 10 = 130'. Line 5: card.
lines: Here's another way. Let's count the sets with a pair directly, in two groups.
Exactly one pair: five colors for the pair.
Then two different colors from the other four, six ways, and a sock of each, four ways.
Five times six times four is one hundred twenty.
Two pairs: choose two of the five colors. There are ten ways.
One hundred twenty plus ten is one hundred thirty. Same answer!
When would you pick this way? It's a great double-check. But the first way didn't need to split into cases.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red. Line 2: 80 = no-pair sets. Line 3: 210 = all. Line 4: '5 × 28 = 140': pick a pair, then any 2 of the other 8 socks. Line 5: one two-pair set (red pair + blue pair) shown being counted twice: once 'red first', once 'blue first'; '140 − 10 = 130'. Line 6: chip 125 red.
lines: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
Choice A says eighty. That's the sets with NO pair, the group we took away.
Choice E, two hundred ten, is every set, before taking any away.
Choice D, one hundred forty, comes from picking a pair, five ways.
Then any two of the other eight socks: eight times seven over two, twenty-eight ways. Five times twenty-eight is one hundred forty.
But a two-pair set gets counted twice, once for each pair.
Take away the ten extras, and you're back to one hundred thirty.
Choice B, one hundred twenty-five, doesn't come from any correct count. Both our methods give one hundred thirty.
So here's a great habit. For at least one, count the opposite and subtract.

scenes.visual: Drawer now has 6 pairs (add a yellow pair): 12 socks.
lines: Ready for a challenge? Now the drawer has six pairs, each a different color.
Zoe pulls out four socks again. How many sets of four contain at least one matching pair?
Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: Rows per line: '12 × 11 × 10 × 9 = 11880', '11880 ÷ 24 = 495'; 'leave out 2 of 6 colors: 15 ways', '15 × 16 = 240'; '495 − 240 = 255' answer badge with chime at end of line 4; check '6 × 10 × 4 = 240', '+ 15 = 255'.
lines: Let's check. Count every set: twelve times eleven times ten times nine, divided by twenty-four.
That's four hundred ninety-five.
No pair: choose four of the six colors.
That's the same as leaving out two colors: six times five over two, fifteen ways. Then sixteen ways to pick the socks.
Fifteen times sixteen is two hundred forty sets with no pair.
Four hundred ninety-five minus two hundred forty is two hundred fifty-five!
Check: one pair gives six times ten times four, two hundred forty, and two pairs gives six times five over two, fifteen.
Two hundred fifty-five again!
If you got two hundred fifty-five, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: 'at least one pair = all − no pair', with sock icons.
lines: Here's the big idea to remember.
When a question says at least one, count the opposite.
Count all the sets, subtract the ones with none, and what's left is your answer.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
